essays.why_software_engineering: I chose software engineering because I love taking messy, manual workflows and turning them into reliable, high-speed systems that people can actually use. Whether I am building a solo full-stack expense tracker for freelancers (Tax Shoebox) where I engineered a cascading cache in TypeScript and Supabase to cut LLM API calls by 85%, or building an automated Python document-processing pipeline at Outamation that cut manual mortgage review time by 75%, I am driven by measurable engineering impact. I enjoy working across the entire stack—from designing normalized PostgreSQL schemas with strict Row-Level Security to shipping responsive React interfaces and testing edge cases with Pytest.
essays.challenging_project: While building Tax Shoebox, a solo full-stack expense-tracking web app for freelancers using TypeScript, React, and Supabase PostgreSQL, I ran into a major cost and latency bottleneck: calling the Claude API to categorize every uploaded receipt line item was slow and expensive at scale. To solve this, I architected a 4-tier cascading categorization cache backed by 7 PostgreSQL schema migrations and 5 Supabase Edge Functions—checking user-specific overrides first, then a shared vendor cache, before falling back to the LLM or deterministic rules. This architecture reduced external LLM inference calls by roughly 85% while maintaining strict tenant data isolation via PostgreSQL Row-Level Security.

behavioral.challenge: At Outamation I built a Python pipeline that extracts structured financial fields from mortgage loan PDFs. The hard part was that scanned pages arrived in noisy, inconsistent layouts, so extraction was unreliable at first. I worked through it methodically: I preprocessed pages with OpenCV, tuned how PyMuPDF and LlamaIndex parsed each layout, and backed every fix with a Pytest regression suite so that solving one layout could not quietly break another. The pipeline reached 95% field-extraction accuracy and cut manual document review time by 75%. It taught me to treat debugging as a measurement problem: reproduce the failure, pin it with a test, then fix it.
behavioral.teamwork: At HackWesTX VI my four-person team built WashBuddy, an AI laundry-sorting web app. My part was integrating the React and Gemini front end with the Node.js/MongoDB backend, which meant agreeing on data shapes with my teammates early and keeping the classification and grouping logic in step with the interface as both changed over the weekend. We shipped an app that sorts clothing by type and fabric across four categories with 94% accuracy and won Best Hack for Beginners. I have also led a team: as Lead Researcher at the Web3 Acceleration Association I directed student researchers analyzing 100+ on-chain transactions and co-authored the paper we presented.
behavioral.initiative: Tax Shoebox started as my own idea and I built it solo, from an empty repository to a working full-stack expense tracker for freelancers filing Schedule C. With no one handing me requirements, I scoped it myself: a TypeScript and React front end on Supabase PostgreSQL, with 7 schema migrations, 5 Edge Functions and row-level security. When calling the Claude API for every receipt line item proved slow and expensive, I designed a 4-tier cascading categorization cache (user override, shared vendor cache, LLM, deterministic fallback) that cut LLM calls by about 85%.
behavioral.learning: As an AI/ML Research Trainee with the Computing Research Association I had an eight-week sprint to become productive with OCR and computer-vision models. I built OCR and vision pipelines to parse, clean and extract text from low-quality scans and photographs, then evaluated and fine-tuned PyTorch vision and NLP architectures across multi-format document layouts, reducing Character Error Rate by 18% on noisy test benchmarks. Working against that deadline taught me to get a baseline running first, measure it, and learn exactly what the next improvement requires.

custom_answers.pattern: favorite c\+\+ feature
custom_answers.answer: RAII. Tying a resource's lifetime to an object's scope means memory, file handles and locks are released deterministically, without a garbage collector and without remembering to clean up on every exit path. My C++ is from coursework at UT Dallas alongside Computer Architecture and Digital Systems, where smart pointers (unique_ptr for single ownership, shared_ptr only when ownership is really shared) made ownership explicit in the type, and where I learned why cache-friendly, contiguous data structures matter. That same concern for predictable performance carried into Project Forge, where I indexed high-frequency lookup columns in PostgreSQL.

custom_answers.pattern: intersection of technology, policy, and ethics
custom_answers.answer: I would work on making automated document decisions auditable. Systems increasingly read people's financial and medical paperwork, and when extraction is wrong the person affected rarely learns why. At Outamation I built a pipeline that extracts fields from mortgage PDFs at 95% accuracy, which also means 5% of fields need a person. My approach would be technical and procedural together: record the evidence behind every extracted value, route low-confidence cases to human review, isolate each person's data (I used PostgreSQL row-level security for this in Tax Shoebox and Project Forge), and give people a way to see and contest what the system read.
